name: Bisu
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Vacharee Nuamkaew 1987. The phonology of the Bisu language as spoken in Chiangrai province (thesis); Xu Shixuan 2001. The Bisu Language — not found online (Payap/SIL 403)

new_statements.quote: Native Bisu syllables (as opposed to Daic loan words) have the canonical form C1 (C2) V T (C3), where C1 represents an obligatory initial consonant, C2 an optional second element in a consonant cluster, V an obligatory vowel, T an obligatory tone, and C3 an optional final consonant. Stress, a relatively minor component of Bisu phonology, does not affect syllable structure. [punctuation normalised from the scanned layer, which renders commas as periods]
new_statements.citation: Person, Kirk R. 2000. Sentence final particles in Bisu narrative. PhD dissertation, University of Texas at Arlington (UMI), 359 pp. §1.4.1 Syllable structure.
new_statements.locator: p. 32, §1.4.1 'Syllable structure' (within §1.4 'Outline of Bisu phonology', pp. 32-38); PDF p. 44 of 359
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bisu is a three-tone register language (low/mid/high; Vacharee 1987 as cited by Person 2000: 36; Nishida 1973: 57-58 gives 55/33/11). Person states only that stress exists and is 'a relatively minor component' of the phonology; no source opened gives a placement rule. The only prominence asymmetry described is Nishida 1973: 59-60 — 'subordinate morphemes following another syllable have a specific tone when they are pronounced carefully, but in normal pronunciation, so-called weak utterances are observed', and 'main syllable + secondary syllable (/la, lə, lɯ, kha/ etc.) + the bound morpheme /-ŋe/' sequences show tone modulation — i.e. reduced (tonally weakened) secondary/bound syllables next to a full main syllable, not a word-stress rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Person 2000 gives no rule at all. Person 2000: 67-68 says Vacharee Nuamkaew's 1987 Mahidol thesis (Pha Daeng dialect) 'presents helpful information about syllable type, stress patterns, and phoneme distribution' — that thesis is the primary source for Bisu stress and could not be opened.
new_statements.domain_note: Person's remark is about syllable structure of the word; Nishida's weakening is a careful-vs-normal speech (phrase-level) phenomenon affecting bound morphemes and secondary syllables. Tone sandhi in verb phrases and particle clusters (Person 2000: 37) is the main suprasegmental process described.
new_statements.identity_note: Person 2000 describes the Thai Bisu of Doi Chomphuu (Amphoe Mae Lao) and Doi Pui (Amphoe Muang), Chiang Rai — the same village Nishida 1966/1973 calls Ban Lua Bisu of Ban Huai San and Bradley calls Huai Chomphu. Kitjapol 2006 Bisu data = Doi Chomphuu. Xu 1998/2001 (not opened) describe the Chinese Bisu (Laomian/Laopin) of Lancang County, Yunnan, which Person 2000: 68 says differs significantly from Thai Bisu. All fall under glottocode bisu1244 (no sub-dialect glottocodes).

No placement rule; three contrastive tones (p. 36, citing Vacharee 1987: 110-115); limited tone sandhi (p. 37). p. 67-68: Vacharee 1987 covers 'syllable type, stress patterns, and phoneme distribution'; p. 68: Beaudouin 1991 has an outline of Bisu phonology; Xu Shixuan (2001) has 'detailed discussion of Bisu phonology'. fetched sources from MPG PuRe REST endpoint (hdl 11858/00-001M-0000-0012-7413-6).

sources.citation: Nishida, Tatsuo. 1973. A preliminary study of the Bisu language: a language of Northern Thailand recently discovered by us. Papers in South East Asian Linguistics No. 3, Pacific Linguistics A-30: 55-82.
sources.note: No stress/accent statement. §4 Toneme pp. 57-59: register tone system, high 55 / mid 33 (laryngeally tense vowel) / low 11 (~21 before pause). p. 59 'Usual pronunciation and careful pronunciation': subordinate morphemes following another syllable keep their tone in careful speech but are 'weak utterances' in normal speech; pp. 59-60 'Modulation phenomena': tone changes in main syllable + secondary syllable (/la, lə, lɯ, kha/) + /-ŋe/ sequences and in main+main sequences. §8 word-units p. 66 (?aŋ- / -ŋe morphology).

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Bisu language' (en) and '毕苏语' (zh), accessed 2026-09-17.
sources.note: en: three tones (mid unmarked, low grave, high acute), no length contrast; nothing on stress. zh: 30 initials, 44 rhymes, three basic tones 31/33/55 plus two non-distinctive tones 22 and 45~35, citing Xu Shixuan 1998 毕苏语研究; no 重音 statement.
